newsitem.title: UK: Oil prices move up on Russian and Iranian jitters.
newsitem.headline: Oil prices move up on Russian and Iranian jitters.

text.p: World oil prices moved higher on Tuesday after Iran threatened to retaliate against the United States in the oil-rich Gulf and partly on concerns over developments in Russia, brokers said.

Underlying market strength was also provided by strong demand for heating oil. Analysts said the first chill of winter was felt on Monday in the U.S. northeast, the world's biggest heating oil market.
Benchmark North Sea Brent blend crude oil futures for November delivery closed 70 cents firmer at $22.95 a barrel.

Brokers in both London and New York said the main market mover on Tuesday was Iran, where Revolutionary Guards commander General Mohsen Rezaei was quoted in the Tehran Times as warning of conflict in the Gulf if confronted with aggressive moves by the United States or Israel.

"What is causing buying pressure is a statement from Iran saying they will engage in conflict with the U.S. and specifically mentioning the Straits of Hormuz," said Michael Rothman, Senior Energy Analyst at Merrill Lynch in New York.
Rothman said that with 10 million barrels per day (bpd) passing through the Gulf strait, the market was jittery about a threat to supply disruptions from the region.
"Action early today is being boosted by Iranian sabre rattling," a London futures broker said.
Prices have held in a tight range since Iraqi leader Saddam Hussein pulled back from a confrontation with the United States, with high demand for heating fuels keeping a floor under prices.

Concerns about Russian President Boris Yeltsin's imminent heart surgery were also mildly supportive in recent days. Russia is the world's third biggest oil producer after Saudi Arabia and the United States.
Industry stocks of heating oil are low, particularly in the U.S. northeast where they are running 19 million barrels below year-ago levels.
"The people in the northeast had to turn on the heat for the first time yesterday. The heating season has commenced," said Rothman.

"Refinery runs start falling off very hard beginning this week. Distillate production will typically decline and last week's jump in refinery runs, if you do a seasonal analysis, represents the last hoorah," he added.

Crude supplies are currently tight despite overproduction by the Organisation of Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC) and the market could have used the 700,000-800,000 bpd of Iraqi oil under the now delayed U.N. oil-for-food deal.
World crude prices rallied to a post-Gulf War high of $24.39 a barrel 10 days ago after the United States fired cruise missiles at Iraqi targets after Iraq intervened in Kurdish factional fighting.

The hostilities prompted the United Nations to postpone implementaiton of the limited oil sales deal, which would have allowed Iraq to resume exports for the first time since sanctions were imposed after its 1990 invasion of Kuwait.
The sustained strength in prices -- Brent is still nearly $5 a barrel more expensive than this time last year -- is bringing windfall revenues to OPEC despite quota busting by some members.
OPEC's quota compliance committee is meeting in Vienna on Wednesday but OPEC sources say little will be done to deal with overproduction as oil prices remain strong and demand buoyant.
Analysts say the group is producing 800,000 bpd above its agreed supply quota of 25.03 million bpd.
